_comment: SURGX evidence index. Each record is OUR OWN explanation of what a source says and why it matters, plus a pointer to the authoritative document. It deliberately does NOT reproduce recommendation tables, algorithms or figures: summarising with attribution is ordinary scholarly use, reproducing the artefact is not ours to do. surgx-evidence.js validateRecord() rejects any record with a `verbatim` field or without an originalSummary.

records.title: The ABCDE primary survey
records.originalSummary: The primary survey exists because injured patients die in a predictable order, and treating problems in that order buys the most time. Its real contribution is not the letters but the discipline: a problem found at A is treated before anyone moves to B, and any deterioration sends you back to the start. The evidence base for the sequence itself is largely observational and consensus-driven; what is well supported is that a standardised, rehearsed team process reduces missed injuries and shortens time to definitive care.

source.org: American College of Surgeons Committee on Trauma
source.title: Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) Student Course Manual

records.title: Damage control resuscitation and the lethal triad
records.originalSummary: Hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy reinforce one another, and each one makes the next harder to correct. The practical consequence is a change in what a first operation is for: control bleeding and contamination, then leave, correct the physiology in intensive care, and return. The associated resuscitation strategy favours early blood components over crystalloid, keeps the patient warm, and accepts a lower blood pressure until the bleeding is controlled. The strongest single piece of evidence in this area is for early antifibrinolytic therapy in traumatic haemorrhage, where the benefit is clearly time-dependent.

source.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
source.title: Major trauma: assessment and initial management (NG39)

records.title: Why source control beats broader antibiotics
records.originalSummary: Antimicrobials work on organisms that are perfused and dividing. Pus, dead tissue, an obstructed duct and a colonised implant are none of those things, which is why a patient failing on an appropriate antibiotic almost never needs a broader one. The consistent finding across intra-abdominal infection literature is that delay to source control, rather than choice of agent, drives mortality. The practical corollary is to choose the least invasive intervention that will actually control the source, and to re-image or re-explore rather than escalate the prescription.

source.title: Guidelines for the management of intra-abdominal infections

records.title: The sepsis bundle, and the surgical element it adds
records.originalSummary: The sepsis bundle is a set of time-bound actions - cultures, antimicrobials, fluid, lactate, vasopressor - whose benefit comes largely from the fact that they happen quickly rather than from any one of them individually. In surgical sepsis there is a sixth element that the general bundle understates: identifying and controlling the anatomical source. The lactate is the most useful repeated measurement, not because it diagnoses anything but because a lactate that will not fall is a source that has not been controlled.

source.title: International guidelines for management of sepsis and septic shock

records.title: The Critical View of Safety
records.originalSummary: The classical bile duct injury happens because the common bile duct is mistaken for the cystic duct, usually after retraction that aligns the two. The Critical View of Safety is a positive confirmation of anatomy rather than a dissection technique: the hepatocystic triangle cleared, the lower third of the gallbladder separated from the cystic plate, and exactly two structures seen entering the gallbladder. Its power is that it is a checkpoint with a defined pass mark, which makes failure to achieve it a recognisable event that triggers a bail-out rather than a slower version of the same dissection.

source.org: Society of American Gastrointestinal and Endoscopic Surgeons (SAGES)
source.title: Safe Cholecystectomy Program: Critical View of Safety and the universal culture of safety

records.title: Grading acute cholecystitis and cholangitis
records.originalSummary: The value of a formal severity grade in biliary sepsis is that it separates three quite different patients who present similarly: the one for early cholecystectomy, the one for percutaneous drainage, and the one whose duct must be decompressed tonight. It also changes the conversation from an impression to a category, which is what makes it possible to hand over. The diagnostic criteria combine local signs, systemic inflammation and imaging, and the associated flowcharts tie each grade to a management pathway.

source.title: Tokyo Guidelines 2018 (TG18) for acute cholangitis and cholecystitis

records.title: Appendicitis: scoring, imaging and the non-operative option
records.originalSummary: Scoring instruments in appendicitis earn their place at both ends: a low score with normal inflammatory markers safely avoids imaging and admission, and a high score in a typical patient supports operating without a CT. Ultrasound has good specificity but poor sensitivity, so a non-visualised appendix is not a negative test. Antibiotic-first management of selected uncomplicated appendicitis is genuinely supported by trial evidence, with a recurrence rate that must be part of the conversation rather than a footnote.

source.title: Diagnosis and treatment of acute appendicitis: Jerusalem guidelines, 2020 update

records.title: Skin and soft-tissue infection: what antibiotics can and cannot do
records.originalSummary: The central distinction is purulent versus non-purulent. A purulent collection is treated by drainage, with antibiotics as an adjunct for surrounding cellulitis, systemic features or immunocompromise. Non-purulent cellulitis is treated with antibiotics and elevation, and the commonest error is treating bilateral lower-leg venous change as infection. Necrotising infection sits outside both: it is a clinical and operative diagnosis, imaging delays it, and the extent of the first debridement is the strongest determinant of survival.

source.title: Practice guidelines for the diagnosis and management of skin and soft tissue infections

records.title: Diabetic foot infection: perfusion, bone and the deep specimen
records.originalSummary: Three things separate a diabetic foot infection from a soft-tissue infection elsewhere. Perfusion must be assessed in every case, because infection does not clear in an ischaemic foot however good the antibiotic. Bone involvement is common and is suggested by a positive probe-to-bone test at the bedside, long before imaging is conclusive. And the specimen that guides therapy is deep tissue or bone, not a superficial swab, which grows colonisers and misdirects treatment for weeks.

source.org: International Working Group on the Diabetic Foot (IWGDF) / IDSA
source.title: Guidelines on the diagnosis and treatment of diabetes-related foot infections

records.title: Upper GI bleeding: risk scores that work in both directions
records.originalSummary: Upper gastrointestinal bleeding is one of the few areas where a pre-endoscopy score reliably identifies a patient who does not need admission at all, as well as one who must not leave the resuscitation room. Two other findings have changed practice more than any drug: a restrictive transfusion strategy improves outcomes outside massive haemorrhage, and in suspected variceal bleeding a splanchnic vasoconstrictor plus antibiotic prophylaxis started before endoscopy improves survival. Proton pump inhibition matters after endoscopy in high-risk non-variceal lesions, not routinely before it.

source.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
source.title: Acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding in over 16s: management

records.title: Groin hernia: tension-free repair and the pain problem
records.originalSummary: Mesh repair reduced recurrence to the point where the dominant long-term complication of groin hernia surgery is no longer recurrence but chronic pain. That reframes the operation: identifying and deliberately handling the three groin nerves is now as important as the mesh itself. The other consistent lesson is about the femoral canal - it must be inspected in every case, particularly in women, because a missed femoral hernia is the one that strangulates. Watchful waiting is a defensible option in minimally symptomatic reducible inguinal hernia in men.

source.title: International guidelines for groin hernia management

records.title: The surgical safety checklist
records.originalSummary: The checklist works less because of the items on it and more because it forces every member of the team to speak once, out loud, before the operation starts. That single change alters whether a scrub practitioner will challenge a surgeon later. Implementation quality matters enormously: a checklist recited while people continue working produces none of the measured benefit, which is why the sign-out - the part most often skipped when a list is running late - is the element most worth defending.

source.title: WHO Surgical Safety Checklist and implementation manual

records.title: Preventing surgical site infection
records.originalSummary: Most surgical site infections come from the patient's own skin and gut flora, which is why the measures that work are unglamorous: an alcohol-based skin preparation allowed to dry, an antibiotic given within the hour before incision and stopped afterwards, normothermia, glycaemic control, and not closing a dirty wound. The measure that does not work, and that is still widely practised, is continuing prophylactic antibiotics for days after a clean operation; it increases resistance without reducing infection.

source.title: Global guidelines for the prevention of surgical site infection, 2nd edition

records.title: Grading surgical complications consistently
records.originalSummary: The Clavien-Dindo classification grades a complication by the treatment it required rather than by how serious it felt, which is what makes it reproducible between surgeons and between units. Its practical value is in audit and in honest conversation: a unit that grades consistently can tell whether its outcomes are changing, and a surgeon who records a grade III has recorded something a reader can interpret without being there.

source.title: Classification of surgical complications: a new proposal with evaluation in a cohort of 6336 patients

records.title: Choosing an empiric regimen in India
records.originalSummary: Empiric antimicrobial choice is a local question wearing the clothes of a global one. National surveillance in India shows resistance patterns, particularly among enteric Gram-negative organisms, that differ substantially from those the international guidelines were written around. The practical rule is to take the syndrome from the guideline and the agent from the local antibiogram, then de-escalate on culture with a documented stop date. StewardMD's own stewardship engine and antibiogram tools exist for exactly this step.

source.title: Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance Network annual report

records.title: Severe traumatic brain injury: thresholds that matter
records.originalSummary: The Brain Trauma Foundation guidelines distil a large but mostly observational literature into a small number of physiological targets. The consistent message is that secondary insults, especially hypotension and hypoxia, are what turn a survivable injury into a poor outcome, so the systolic pressure floors are age-banded and set higher than for general trauma. Intracranial pressure is treated above 22 mmHg and cerebral perfusion is aimed at roughly 60 to 70 mmHg, but the evidence for any single number is modest, and the guidelines are better read as a framework than as a protocol. Interventions with consistent evidence of harm, such as steroids and prolonged prophylactic hyperventilation, are explicitly discouraged.

source.title: Guidelines for the management of severe traumatic brain injury, 4th edition

records.title: Decompressive craniectomy for refractory intracranial hypertension
records.originalSummary: RESCUEicp randomised patients with traumatic brain injury and intracranial pressure that stayed high despite tiered medical therapy to a large decompressive craniectomy or continued medical care. Surgery substantially reduced mortality, but many of the extra survivors lived with severe disability or in a vegetative state. The trial reframes craniectomy as a values decision rather than a purely technical one: it saves lives, and the family needs to understand the range of outcomes it produces. It was a last-tier intervention in this trial, which differs from the earlier DECRA trial, where early bifrontal craniectomy for diffuse injury did not improve functional outcome.

source.title: Trial of decompressive craniectomy for traumatic intracranial hypertension (N Engl J Med 2016;375:1119-30)

records.title: Drains after burr-hole drainage of chronic subdural haematoma
records.originalSummary: In a single-centre randomised trial, placing a drain in the subdural space after burr-hole evacuation of a chronic subdural haematoma reduced recurrence needing further surgery to well under half of the rate seen without a drain, and was associated with lower six-month mortality, without an increase in complications. The finding changed practice, making a drain the default unless the surgeon has a specific reason not to place one. A later national trial of adjuvant dexamethasone found it worsened functional outcome, so steroids are not a routine part of this pathway.

source.org: Santarius T et al, The Lancet
source.title: Use of drains versus no drains after burr-hole evacuation of chronic subdural haematoma: a randomised controlled trial (Lancet 2009;374:1067-73)

records.title: Coiling versus clipping for ruptured aneurysms
records.originalSummary: ISAT randomised patients with ruptured aneurysms judged suitable for either treatment to endovascular coiling or neurosurgical clipping. At one year, fewer coiled patients were dead or dependent. The advantage came with a higher rate of late rebleeding and retreatment after coiling, which is why long-term imaging follow-up matters. The trial population was mostly good-grade patients with small anterior circulation aneurysms, so the result does not settle the choice for every aneurysm; it supports a joint decision between neurosurgeon and interventional neuroradiologist for each patient.

source.org: International Subarachnoid Aneurysm Trial (ISAT) Collaborative Group
source.title: International Subarachnoid Aneurysm Trial of neurosurgical clipping versus endovascular coiling in 2143 patients with ruptured intracranial aneurysms (Lancet 2002;360:1267-74)

records.title: Surgery plus radiotherapy for metastatic cord compression
records.originalSummary: Patchell and colleagues randomised patients with spinal cord compression from metastatic cancer at a single area to direct decompressive surgery followed by radiotherapy, or radiotherapy alone. More patients in the surgical group walked after treatment, kept walking for longer, and regained walking if they had lost it. The trial excluded very radiosensitive tumours and patients with short life expectancy, so the result applies to selected patients. Its lasting lesson is that walking ability is the outcome to protect, and that surgical opinion should be sought early rather than after radiotherapy has failed.

source.org: Patchell RA et al, The Lancet
source.title: Direct decompressive surgical resection in the treatment of spinal cord compression caused by metastatic cancer: a randomised trial (Lancet 2005;366:643-48)

records.title: The national suspected cauda equina pathway
records.originalSummary: The GIRFT national pathway for suspected cauda equina syndrome responds to a pattern of delayed diagnosis and avoidable harm. It treats suspected CES as an emergency at any hour, expects emergency MRI without waiting for a routine list, and asks that patients with confirmed compression go to surgery promptly. It also emphasises clear documentation of saddle sensation and bladder function, communicating results to the patient, and safety-netting those whose scans are normal. Its value is less in any single new finding than in removing the overnight and weekend delays that drive poor outcomes.

source.org: Getting It Right First Time (GIRFT), NHS England
source.title: National suspected cauda equina syndrome (CES) pathway

records.title: Decompression before stone treatment in the obstructed infected kidney
records.originalSummary: An infected, obstructed collecting system behaves like an abscess: antibiotics cannot reach adequate concentrations in urine that is not draining, so the kidney must be decompressed urgently. European guidance treats percutaneous nephrostomy and retrograde ureteric stenting as equally effective for this purpose, leaving the choice to local availability and the patient's anatomy and fitness. The stone itself is left alone until the infection has been treated, because instrumenting an infected system can precipitate severe sepsis. Cultures from the renal pelvis taken at drainage often differ from bladder urine and should guide the antibiotic course. The practical lesson is about time: the route that drains the kidney soonest and most safely tonight is the right one.

source.title: EAU Guidelines on Urolithiasis

records.title: Imaging, analgesia and timing in renal colic
records.originalSummary: The UK national guideline for stones sets out a simple pathway for adults with suspected ureteric colic: low-dose non-contrast CT within a day of presentation, brought forward when there is fever, a solitary kidney or real diagnostic doubt, with ultrasound first in pregnancy and in children. For pain, a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug by any route comes first, intravenous paracetamol is the alternative, and opioids are reserved for when both are unsuitable. Alpha-blockers are offered for smaller distal ureteric stones. For stones that are unlikely to pass or pain that is not tolerated, the guideline expects definitive treatment within a short window rather than prolonged waiting. Its value is in making these timings explicit and auditable.

source.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
source.title: Renal and ureteric stones: assessment and management (NG118)

records.title: A clinical score for testicular torsion
records.originalSummary: This paediatric study derived and validated a short bedside score for testicular torsion from five findings: testicular swelling, a hard testis, an absent cremasteric reflex, nausea or vomiting, and a high-riding testis. Its practical contribution is to give the examining clinician permission to act: children with a high score had torsion often enough to justify going directly to theatre without ultrasound, while those with a low score were unlikely to have it. The middle group is where imaging helps most. The score supports, but never replaces, the surgeon's judgement, and a worried surgeon should still explore a child with a low score. External validation studies have generally supported it, with lower performance when applied by less experienced examiners.

source.org: The Journal of Urology (Barbosa JA et al.)
source.title: Development and initial validation of a scoring system to diagnose testicular torsion in children

records.title: Irrigant absorption and TUR syndrome
records.originalSummary: This review explains how irrigating fluid enters the circulation during endoscopic surgery, mostly through opened venous sinuses and perforations, and how the effects depend on the fluid. With hypotonic, electrolyte-free solutions such as glycine used for monopolar resection, large absorption causes dilutional hyponatraemia, fluid overload and, with glycine, direct neurological and visual effects. Risk rises with longer resection, higher irrigation pressure, and capsular or bladder perforation. The review supports practical measures: low-pressure irrigation, attention to resection time, monitoring of absorption where possible, and early sodium measurement when symptoms appear. Bipolar resection in saline removes the hyponatraemic mechanism, though large-volume absorption can still overload the circulation.

source.title: Fluid absorption in endoscopic surgery

records.title: Non-operative management of renal trauma
records.originalSummary: Contemporary trauma and urology guidance converge on one principle: in a haemodynamically stable patient, renal injury of almost any grade is managed without surgery, with contrast CT including a delayed phase to stage it and angioembolisation for active bleeding, pseudoaneurysm or fistula. The 2018 revision of the organ injury scale added vascular findings on CT to the grading, which aligns the grade more closely with what interventional radiology can treat. Exploration is reserved for physiology that does not respond to resuscitation because of the kidney, or an expanding or pulsatile retroperitoneal haematoma at laparotomy. This approach has substantially reduced nephrectomy rates without worsening outcomes.

source.org: World Society of Emergency Surgery (WSES) and AAST (Coccolini F et al., World Journal of Emergency Surgery)
source.title: Kidney and uro-trauma: WSES-AAST guidelines

records.title: TURBT quality: muscle in the specimen and early instillation
records.originalSummary: European bladder cancer guidance treats the first resection as the most important staging event in the disease. A complete resection with detrusor muscle in the specimen is needed to tell non-invasive from invasive disease, and its absence is itself an indication for early re-resection in most cases. Recording the number, size and site of tumours, and sending the base separately, improve the information the pathologist can return. A single immediate post-operative chemotherapy instillation reduces recurrence in appropriately selected tumours, but it is withheld when a perforation is suspected or there is significant bleeding. Enhanced cystoscopy improves detection of small and flat lesions where it is available.

source.title: EAU Guidelines on Non-muscle-invasive Bladder Cancer

records.title: Why green vomit in a baby is an emergency
records.originalSummary: Malrotation leaves the midgut hanging on a narrow mesenteric pedicle that can twist, cutting off the blood supply to most of the small bowel within hours. Bile-stained vomiting is often the only early sign, and the abdomen may be soft and the baby may look well. The radiology appropriateness criteria place the upper gastrointestinal contrast study as the key test because it shows where the duodenojejunal flexure lies; ultrasound signs can support it but do not replace it when there is doubt. The practical consequence is a low threshold: many negative studies are an acceptable price for not missing a volvulus, and a shocked or peritonitic baby goes to theatre without waiting for imaging.

source.title: ACR Appropriateness Criteria: Vomiting in infants (J Am Coll Radiol 2020;17(11S):S505-S515)

records.title: Open or laparoscopic pyloromyotomy
records.originalSummary: Randomised trials comparing open and laparoscopic pyloromyotomy are few and small, and pooled analysis gives low-certainty evidence. Neither approach is clearly safer overall. There is a signal, with wide uncertainty, that laparoscopy may slightly increase the chance of an incomplete myotomy or mucosal perforation, while recovery differences are measured in hours. For the surgeon this means the choice is reasonably made on local expertise, and that whichever route is used, a complete myotomy and a deliberate leak test matter more than the access. The bigger safety lever sits before theatre: correcting the alkalosis and dehydration.

source.title: Open versus laparoscopic pyloromyotomy for pyloric stenosis (Staerkle et al, CD012827)

records.title: Getting intussusception reduced without an operation
records.originalSummary: A systematic review by the American Pediatric Surgical Association looked at how stable children with intussusception are best managed. Its main messages are practical: routine antibiotics before enema reduction do not reduce complications; a second, delayed enema is reasonable when the first only partly reduces the intussusception and the child remains well; many children can be observed briefly and discharged after successful reduction rather than admitted; and when surgery is needed, laparoscopic reduction often succeeds and avoids a laparotomy. The evidence is mostly observational, so these are best read as permission to be less invasive in a stable child, not as a reason to persist with enemas in a sick one.

source.org: American Pediatric Surgical Association (APSA) Outcomes and Evidence Based Practice Committee
source.title: Management of intussusception in children: a systematic review (J Pediatr Surg 2021;56(3):587-596)

records.title: Which injured child needs a head CT
records.originalSummary: The PECARN study followed tens of thousands of children with minor head trauma and derived and validated separate rules for children under and over two years of age. The rules are designed to find children at very low risk of a clinically important brain injury, in whom CT can be avoided, and to separate an intermediate group for whom observation is a reasonable alternative to immediate scanning. Their value is in reducing radiation exposure in a population where most head injuries are trivial. They apply only to children with a near-normal conscious level; a child with a reduced score is scanned regardless.

source.org: Pediatric Emergency Care Applied Research Network (PECARN)
source.title: Identification of children at very low risk of clinically-important brain injuries after head trauma (Lancet 2009;374:1160-70)

records.title: Ectopic pregnancy: who needs surgery and which operation
records.originalSummary: The NICE guideline separates women with ectopic pregnancy into those who can be offered methotrexate, those who need surgery, and those for whom either is reasonable, using pain, the size of the mass, the presence of a heartbeat and the hCG level. Rupture with haemodynamic compromise is always surgical. Laparoscopy is preferred, and salpingectomy is the default unless the other tube is damaged, in which case salpingotomy may preserve fertility at the price of closer hCG follow-up for persistent trophoblast. The guideline also asks for anti-D for rhesus-negative women having surgical management, and for proper information and support after a pregnancy loss.

source.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
source.title: Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage: diagnosis and initial management (NG126)

records.title: Climbing the postpartum haemorrhage ladder quickly
records.originalSummary: The RCOG guidance frames major postpartum haemorrhage as a team emergency with parallel work: communication, resuscitation, monitoring and arresting the bleeding all at once. Uterotonic drugs are used in sequence, and when they fail the guidance favours moving to surgery sooner rather than later. Balloon tamponade is the first surgical step for atony, followed by compression sutures, devascularisation and radiological embolisation where available, and hysterectomy without delay when conservative measures fail, especially with accreta or rupture. Separate trial evidence underpins early tranexamic acid, whose benefit is greatest when given within three hours of birth.

source.org: Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG)
source.title: Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage (Green-top Guideline No. 52)
